items_missed: Never asked "How are you today?" style check-in at the open.
Skipped several probe items: special considerations (narrow hallways/turns), packing needs, box count, storage stops, and moving stressors were never asked.
Never stated the actual hourly rate ($/mover/hour) or what's bundled into it (gas, truck, taxes, tools, wrap pads) — jumped straight to a lump total estimate ($800-$1,000).
Skipped the "pricing is super simple" framing and the full no-hidden-fees pitch (no credit card fee, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fee).
Never mentioned the On-Time Guarantee (automatic discounting if the arrival window is missed), despite giving a 30-minute arrival window.
Estimate wasn't broken down by variables — no mention of the three-story origin's stairs, walk distance, drive time, or assembly/disassembly as factors behind the 4-5 hour range.
Entire Save Your Ass prep speech was skipped — no consolidation tips (toys, drawers, garage items) and no "take a carload" advice, despite this being an hourly-billed move.
Didn't explicitly say "no deposit required," even while discussing rescheduling/cancellation flexibility.
Used the customer's name only once, at the very end ("Aaron") — short of the 3+ target.
Insurance explanation covered the $2,000 No Worries coverage but omitted the 60¢/lb standard valuation baseline comparison.
top_strength: Nicole ran a clean, well-organized reconfirmation call: she accurately recapped every detail already on file (both addresses, home size, parking access, appliances), caught and reconciled the customer's own contradictions in real time (three-story vs. "two bedroom" then "one bedroom"), and walked through the clock/minimum/billing mechanics clearly enough that the customer had zero follow-up cost questions.
coaching_note: The single highest-leverage fix: Nicole skipped the Save Your Ass prep speech entirely on a move that's billed by the hour — a quick consolidation/"take a carload" tip before the close costs nothing and directly shortens the billed time for this customer.
phone_presence_notes: Frequent natural affirmations ("Awesome," "Oh, I see," "Thank you so much") and warm acknowledgment of the customer's corrections kept the tone comfortable and the customer ended the call saying she was "excited," though the repeated "Awesome" verges on scripted and there's no standout rapport or humor moment.
